findings.body:
**SSRF: host allowlist removed for customer-provided webhook URLs.**

`deliver()` used to resolve the URL hostname and reject anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. That gate is gone, so any caller-supplied `url` is fetched server-side via `urllib.request.urlopen`.

If a customer (or an attacker who can set the webhook URL) configures `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://127.0.0.1:<internal-port>/`, or another private/internal host, this process will POST the event payload there and return the response status — full SSRF from the delivery path.

Restoring customer endpoints safely needs an egress policy before `urlopen`, for example: HTTPS-only, block loopback/private/link-local/metadata ranges (and DNS rebinding), plus an optional per-tenant allowlist. Do not ship open URL fetch as the enterprise feature.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only host allowlist on outbound webhook delivery and turns customer-configured URLs into an open SSRF primitive.

## Findings

| # | Severity | File | Summary |
|---|----------|------|---------|
| 1 | 🚨 critical | `webhooks.py:4` | Host allowlist removed; arbitrary customer URLs enable SSRF |

## Details

`deliver()` previously rejected any URL whose hostname was outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`hooks.internal.example`). The PR deletes that check and posts to whatever `url` the caller passes.

Concrete failure mode: a customer (or anyone who can set the webhook URL) supplies `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://127.0.0.1:6379/`, or an internal admin host. The runner then issues a server-side POST with the event body and returns the status — classic SSRF against cloud metadata, localhost, and private network services.

Supporting customer endpoints is a valid product goal, but it needs an explicit egress policy (HTTPS-only, DNS rebinding protections, block private/link-local/metadata ranges, optional per-tenant allowlist), not deletion of the existing gate.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes
